b: Bassam Tariq's audacious thriller finds the absurdity and unexpected tenderness in the business of being a man.

There are many ways to fail as a parent, but few quite so unusually humiliating as fighting your way through a roomful of armed men only to spill your dwindling supply of breast milk. But heightened realities surrounding mundane disappointments is par for the course in Bassam Tariq’s Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, where Mahershala Ali plays a man whose professional killer skills border on the supernatural, while his domestic and spiritual lives teeter perpetually on the brink of collapse. For all its magnificently choreographed bloodshed, mordant wit and intricate characterisations, this is a tale of hard-won humility.

Failure, as it happens, is also responsible for the film’s existence. Tariq and Ali wasted years developing Marvel’s Blade, a superhero blockbuster that never even began production, (despite Kevin Feige somehow finding the resources to drag Michael Douglas kicking and screaming into a third Ant-Man). Their eventual collaboration goes some way towards compensating for that indignity. It remains criminal that two-time Oscar winner Ali has been such an infrequent fixture at the cinema while languishing in development hell, but it’s difficult to imagine Blade being half as good as one they have finally made together.

Ali’s Latif is a widowed Muslim assassin raising three children in Houston, where a conflict between Arab Muslim pornographers and evangelical anti-porn crusaders is escalating. John Cho plays a former Marine whose Christian morality is, as one might expect, very selective. Latif, however, wants no part of it. Exhausted by Ramadan, his greatest concern is that his newborn daughter refuses formula, and the supply of frozen breast milk left by his late wife is running out. Tariq has effectively invented an action-movie MacGuffin that needs replenishing every three hours, turning the logistics of infant feeding into a source of unbearable, endlessly renewable, suspense. Beneath the absurdity lies a particularly cruel metaphor: the milk is the last tangible remnant of his beloved wife, disappearing one sachet at a time.

Ali is, to absolutely no one’s surprise, magnificent. He locates the character’s contradictions in the smallest physical details, whether negotiating safety, preparing for danger or reluctantly dispatching henchmen with his sword. Yet the same body becomes awkward and ungainly in the presence of his grieving children. Tariq's attention to nuance extends beyond his leading man, into wonderful turns from Adia as his quick-witted grieving daughter, Tramell Tillman as his unimpressed brother-in-law, Giancarlo Esposito as his world weary imam and Abubakr Ali as his posturing student turned Adult content creator. However, even to those unfortunate enough to find themselves on the wrong end of Latif's sword, Tariq refuses the comforting fiction that anonymous henchmen are somehow less alive, or less dead, than everyone else. His action sequences are thrilling, but their victims suffer with a specificity that makes the thrills feel faintly incriminating.

For all its bloody spectacle, Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is most interested in the failures that cannot be corrected through brute force. Latif can punish the people responsible for his family's suffering, but he cannot make his children suffer less. He can save his former student but he cannot force him to become a decent human being. He can avenge his imam but cannot forgive God for taking his wife. The film's great achievement is to make these failures feel more consequential than any of its spectacular victories. It's a rare, gorgeous action film in which the emotional stakes don't just justify the spectacle, but comprehensively upstage it.
